name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,295

entries.clue: Novelist means to track man with Chinese porcelain (9)

indicators.note: to track someone is to follow behind them, so the means comes after the other pieces

blocks.note: a man is referred to as he
Ming vases come from the Ming dynasty
a means of doing something is a way

annotation.surface: A novelist tracking down a man who owns a Chinese vase.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads the means first, but 'to track' puts it behind the man and the porcelain.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Ernest Hemingway, author of The Old Man and the Sea, is one novelist among many.

entries.clue: Had me and cast developed using manual skills? (8)

indicators.note: to cast is to pour into a mould and give a new shape, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: Someone boasting that they and a cast of actors grew by working with their hands.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is taken letter for letter, and 'cast' reads like a theatre cast rather than an instruction to remould.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: something made by hand rather than machine has been produced using manual skills.

entries.clue: Pot noodle (3)

blocks.note: a drinking vessel with a handle
slang for the head or face

annotation.surface: An instant snack in a cup.
annotation.walkthrough: Together the words suggest a Pot Noodle, a British brand of instant noodles in a cup; separately each is a definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a mug is a pot for tea, and mug, like noodle, is slang for the face or head, as in 'ugly mug'.

entries.clue: Circle filling part of body? Hangman uses this (5)

indicators.note: a filling sits inside something, as in a sandwich, so the circle goes inside the body part

blocks.note: the nose is part of the body
the letter O is a circle

annotation.surface: A riddle about a ring on the body leading to the gallows.
annotation.walkthrough: The circle sits after the first two letters of the body part.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the looped rope is the hangman's tool, so the whole phrase stands for it.

entries.clue: Women’s rowing team boosting sport (13)

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for women
a racing crew of eight rowers is an eight
boosting means lifting

annotation.surface: A women's rowing crew giving their sport a lift.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boosting' looks like a verb acting on 'sport', but it is just the last piece.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: weightlifting is one sport among many, contested at the Olympics.

entries.clue: I accept that our time will come after year (5,2)

indicators.note: coming after means following in sequence, so the year is placed first

blocks.note: Y is the abbreviation for year
taken as it stands
an eon is a long period of time

annotation.surface: A confident prediction that our moment will arrive after a year.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Our' is used as printed, while 'time' means an age.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the phrase is said when taking up a bet or challenge, so it amounts to "I accept".

entries.clue: Modest attempt (3)

blocks.note: bashful, reserved
a throw or go at something, as at a fairground stall

annotation.surface: A half-hearted try.
annotation.walkthrough: Together the words read as a small try; apart, each is a definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain senses: bashful, and a throw or try, as in a coconut shy at a fair.

entries.clue: Dodgy sweet and sour producing wind (9)

indicators.note: dodgy means unsound or unreliable, so the letters cannot be trusted to stay in order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange; 'and' only joins the two words

annotation.surface: A suspect sweet and sour takeaway causing flatulence.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is digestive: 'wind' reads as flatulence, but it is the weather sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain sense: a sou'wester is a wind blowing from the south-west.

entries.clue: Cry, lacking courage, emitting “ow” (4)

indicators.note: to emit is to send out, so the quoted letters are sent out of the word

blocks.note: yellow is slang for cowardly
taken as printed and removed

annotation.surface: A cowardly person crying out in pain.
annotation.walkthrough: The quoted 'ow' looks like the cry itself, but it is the part thrown away.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cry and a yell are both loud shouts.

entries.clue: Cocktail Ronnie mixed with a drop of gin (7)

indicators.note: mixing a drink stirs its ingredients together, so the letters are stirred
a drop is the smallest amount, so only the first letter of gin goes in

blocks.note: taken as printed
the first letter of gin

annotation.surface: Someone called Ronnie mixing a drink with a splash of gin.
annotation.walkthrough: Ronnie reads like a bartender, but his name is the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the negroni, gin with vermouth and Campari, is one cocktail among many.

entries.clue: American university lecturer initially following a routine (5)

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter of lecturer
following means coming after, so the lecturer's letter goes after the a

blocks.note: US is short for American
U is the abbreviation for university
taken as printed
the first letter of lecturer

annotation.surface: An American academic sticking to a set routine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Following a routine' reads as one phrase, but 'a' is a piece and 'routine' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: as adjectives, routine and usual both mean ordinary and customary.

entries.clue: Encountered army corps just beyond the yard (5)

blocks.note: encountered means met
RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army

annotation.surface: Soldiers met just past the back garden.
annotation.walkthrough: The yard looks like a garden, but it is the unit of length.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a metre is about 39 inches, a little over the 36-inch yard.

entries.clue: Severely criticise Kate changing a role (4,5)

indicators.note: changing something alters it, so Kate's letters are altered in order

blocks.note: Kate's letters rearranged
taken as printed
an actor's role is a part

annotation.surface: An actress named Kate being slated for switching roles.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Changing' seems to go with 'a role', but it only acts on Kate.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to take apart a performance or argument is to criticise it severely, as if dismantling it.

entries.clue: Dog doctor on the radio (6)

indicators.note: radio is heard, not seen, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a doctor is a healer

annotation.surface: A vet with a radio phone-in show.
annotation.walkthrough: Dog doctor suggests a vet, but 'Dog' is the definition on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the heeler is a cattle dog breed that herds by nipping at heels.

entries.clue: Old relative keeps recording style of garment (3,5)

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so the relative holds the recording

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a niece is a relative
an extended-play record

annotation.surface: An elderly relative holding on to a recording of how clothes used to be styled.
annotation.walkthrough: An extended-play record, longer than a single but shorter than an album, is a stock crossword recording; it splits the relative after her first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: a one-piece, such as a swimsuit or jumpsuit, is a garment style made as a single piece.

entries.clue: Aristocrat somewhere in New Zealand leaving wife for jazz musician (4,9)

indicators.note: leaving a place means going out of it, so the wife's letter goes out of the city

blocks.note: a duke is an aristocrat
Wellington is New Zealand's capital
W is the abbreviation for wife, removed

annotation.surface: A nobleman in New Zealand leaving his wife for a jazz player.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a society scandal, but the wife leaving is just one letter dropping out of the city.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Duke Ellington, the bandleader behind Take the A Train, is one jazz musician among many.

entries.clue: College pupil from north European country, not south (7)

indicators.note: 'not south' denies the south its place, so the word is written without that letter

blocks.note: Estonian means from Estonia
S is the abbreviation for south, removed

annotation.surface: A student arriving from a Baltic country rather than a southern one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'From ... country' asks for the adjective of the country, not its name.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: Eton College is an English private school, and its pupils are known as Etonians.

entries.clue: Sack amateur belonging to force (3,3)

blocks.note: lay means non-professional
of expresses belonging
F is the symbol for force in physics

annotation.surface: Dismissing a volunteer from the police force.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Force' looks like the police, but it is the physics symbol.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to lay off staff is to dismiss them, often for lack of work, which is the verb sense of sack.

entries.clue: Paddy left son going back (5)

indicators.note: going back means travelling backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: port is the left side of a ship
S is the abbreviation for son

annotation.surface: Paddy departing after his son heads home.
annotation.walkthrough: Paddy looks like a man's name; here it is a British word for a temper tantrum.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional synonym: paddy and strop are both British words for a fit of bad temper.

entries.clue: Begin small pastry dish (5)

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a tart is a pastry dish

annotation.surface: An instruction to open a meal with a little pastry.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a menu starter; the size abbreviation simply joins the pastry.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to set something going or get under way.

entries.clue: Commanding Officer visiting Afghan maybe (4)

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for Commanding Officer
visiting a place is being at it

annotation.surface: A military commander visiting an Afghan person.
annotation.walkthrough: Afghan seems to be a person, but an afghan is also a long sheepskin garment.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'maybe': an afghan is one kind of sheepskin coat.

entries.clue: African animal fine alongside a Greek character (5)

indicators.note: alongside means next to, so the pieces are set side by side

blocks.note: fine means OK
taken as printed
pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

annotation.surface: An African animal doing well beside a Greek.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' means a letter here, not a person.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the okapi, a forest relative of the giraffe from Congo, is one African animal.

entries.clue: Furious with a kid in middle of diner (2,1,4)

indicators.note: 'in' places one thing inside another, as a person is in a room
the middle of a word is what remains without its first and last letters

blocks.note: diner without its outer letters
taken as printed
to kid is to tease, or rag

annotation.surface: An angry parent with a child in the middle of a restaurant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a child, but it is the verb meaning tease.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to be in a rage is to be furious, the phrase working as an adjective.

entries.clue: Turkish officer appearing in gangway at regular intervals (3)

indicators.note: appearing in means showing up inside, so the letters come from within gangway
evenly spaced, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

annotation.surface: A Turkish officer standing in the aisle every so often.
annotation.walkthrough: Gangway's even letters give the title; the odd ones are discarded.
annotation.definitionFit: A historical sense: an aga, or agha, was a military commander in the Ottoman Empire.

entries.clue: Stuart regularly avoided tasteless stuff (3)

indicators.note: letters avoided at regular spacing are skipped, so every other one is dropped

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

annotation.surface: Someone called Stuart steering clear of tacky goods.
annotation.walkthrough: Stuart's first, third and fifth letters are the ones avoided.
annotation.definitionFit: A British colloquialism: tat means cheap, tasteless goods or junk.

entries.clue: Dark horse’s dreadful experience (9)

blocks.note: read literally, a female horse of the dark hours
a horribly bad ordeal

annotation.surface: An unexpected winner's awful ordeal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dark horse' is an idiom for an unexpected contender, but here it is read word by word.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: literally a horse of the dark, and figuratively any ordeal as frightening as a bad dream.
